title: Knowledge Check 8: Lessons 57-60
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 57-60 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: WCAG is organized around four principles rather than a symptom list. Which of these is one of those four principles?
options: Perceivable
Optimized
Consistent
Responsive
questions.explanation: WCAG's four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. They are the load-bearing structure of the standard: every success criterion is an expression of one of them.

questions.question: An architect wants a custom status badge that shows an overdue flag using red color alone, because the team likes a color-only presentation. Based on the lesson, which design requirement rules this out?
options: Meaning must not be conveyed by color alone.
All text must meet a 7:1 contrast ratio.
Every badge must use a Lightning base component.
The badge must announce via an aria-live region.
questions.explanation: The perceivability principle and contrast criteria require that color is not the only channel for meaning. The fix is to pair the red with text and an icon that has a text alternative, and to check the red against the 4.5:1 ratio for small text.

questions.question: Why does choosing a Lightning base component resolve most contrast and keyboard work in a Salesforce build?
options: Because base components disable custom styling entirely.
Because base components contain accessible SLDS markup, follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, and meet or exceed WCAG 2.1 AA contrast.
Because base components automatically pass all WCAG AAA criteria.
Because base components replace the need for real form labels.
questions.explanation: Base components include accessible HTML markup from SLDS, follow the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide for keyboard behavior and ARIA management, and conform to SLDS color guidelines that meet or exceed WCAG 2.1 AA contrast. That is why preferring base components is the highest-leverage accessibility decision.

questions.question: An architect drafts an NFR that reads "the order page should be fast." Based on the lesson, why does this fail as a non-functional requirement?
options: Because it relates to functionality rather than a quality of the solution.
Because it names no quantity, number, and condition, so no test or reviewer can verify it.
Because the platform SLA already covers response time for customer-facing pages.
Because response time is not a quality that a Salesforce solution can control.
questions.explanation: The lesson's test for a good NFR is that it names a quantity, a number, and a condition. "Should be fast" names none of them, so every reader interprets it differently and no test can be built for it. The measurable form is a target such as "returns a confirmation within two seconds for ninety percent of users at expected peak volume."

questions.question: A customer-facing Experience Cloud order flow calls an external inventory API. The architect writes a reliability NFR but cannot decide between setting a recovery time objective (RTO) and a recovery point objective (RPO). Which statement correctly applies both from the lesson?
options: RPO is how long the solution can be down, and RTO is how much data the business accepts losing.
RTO is how long the solution can be down, and RPO is how much data the business accepts losing; both together define how the solution behaves when something goes wrong.
RTO and RPO are the same target measured at different points in the flow.
An integration callout is covered entirely by the Salesforce platform SLA, so the architect need not set either.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines RTO as how long the solution can be down and RPO as how much data the business accepts losing, and notes that these recovery targets determine how a system behaves when things go wrong. They translate directly into design choices, such as whether a data replication or backup strategy is required.

questions.question: An architect wants the build team to implement an order flow and realizes a stock check can fail or time out. Which sequence diagram technique from the lesson forces the architect to decide, on paper, what happens on the failure path?
options: Adding every participant as a lifeline in the "instance name : class name" form.
Including every return message on a dotted line with an open arrowhead.
Adding an alternative combined fragment labeled "alt" whose guards route to a confirmed path and a manual-review path.
Renaming the frame so it begins with "sd" instead of another diagram type.
questions.explanation: An alternative combined fragment, labeled "alt", models if-then-else logic: it sends one set of messages when a guard is true and a different set otherwise. Drawing the happy path and the failure path inside an alt fragment forces the architect to decide what happens when the third-party system is slow or down, which is the decision that is painful to make for the first time during an incident.

questions.question: A team plans a synchronous integration where the external system sits directly on the submission transaction's critical path. The board spots that three follow-on consumers are due next quarter and steers the design to an event-driven path. Which lesson point best explains why the presenter is expected to respond constructively rather than defensively?
options: Because a synchronous callout is forbidden by the platform's governor limits, so there is no valid defense to offer.

Because a board review tests whether the presenter has thought through the implications and prepared alternatives, and the reviews of a design are the security against future failures, so the presenter weighs the new cost on the record and revises if it flips the balance.
Because the board's decision is final and irreversible, so arguing any point is a waste of the presenter's credibility.
Because the event-driven option is always faster to implement, so the synchronous design was wrong from the start.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames a hard board question as a signal to weigh the concern on the record, not to protect identity. The presenter had prepared the coupling tradeoff between the synchronous callout and the event-driven option, so when the board surfaced the three follow-on consumers, they could honestly weigh that cost and revise the recommendation before being forced to. The board is trying to prevent future disasters, not kill the project.

questions.question: An architect is preparing a design to take to the ARB. Which activity best matches the lesson's guidance for defending tradeoffs?
options: Writing a polished slide deck that states the recommendation and omits the alternatives, so the board does not get confused.
Listing at least two alternatives for every major choice and being ready to explain why each was rejected and what the chosen option gives up.
Memorizing answers to likely questions so every response sounds confident, including values the architect has not actually verified.
Waiting until the review to see which direction the board favors, then agreeing with the majority to save time.
questions.explanation: The lesson's prepared-mind guidance is that for every major decision the presenter should know at least two alternatives, why they were rejected, and what was traded to pick the chosen one. Prepared slides alone are not enough; a prepared mind runs the hard questions before the meeting. Presenting a recommendation with no alternatives, or inventing a confident-but-unverified value, directly contradicts the lesson.

questions.question: The ARB grants a design a temporary departure from a sandbox policy so a pilot tool can be used. What must the board do to keep this a real exception rather than a permanent hole in governance?
options: Accept the paper record of the meeting and rely on memory to revisit the policy later.
Grant the exception for an open-ended period so the pilot team is not blocked by review.
Set an expiration date on the exception and own the follow-up re-review, because an exception granted indefinitely becomes a permanent gap nobody remembers granting.
Require the pilot to continue past the stated end date so the team can fully evaluate the tool.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that exceptions should expire: they exist to accommodate a temporary nonconformance while the team plans and implements a better long-term solution, so the board sets an expiration date and an owner for the re-review. An indefinite exception is a permanent hole in governance, which is exactly the failure an exception process is meant to avoid.

questions.question: You open a design review for a new case-resolution agent with a live demo of it answering a support question. A senior reviewer pushes back that the demo is not a review artifact. Which opening would have been the stronger way to present the design?
options: Demonstrate the agent across several different sample cases to show its range
Lead with the evaluation plan: the evidence the system works, how it was gathered, and where the evidence has holes
Show the model benchmark that scored highest on the training dataset
Confirm that the agent's output is deterministic and repeatable across runs
questions.explanation: The lesson holds that the first thing to bring to a review is not a demo but an evaluation plan. An AI system has no single behavior to defend, so the presenter leads with how the system's expected behavior was measured and where that evidence is thin.

questions.question: An agent's logs flag a session as a successful task completion, but reading the transcript shows the user got an answer that did not actually resolve their request. This is a patient user who may quietly go back to a manual workflow. What severity tier does this interaction belong to, and what does it illustrate?
options: P0, trust-breaking, because the answer was wrong and the user lost faith
P1, intent failure, because a technically accurate answer was still not useful enough to complete the task
P2, friction, because the answer was correct but delivered inconveniently
It is not a failure, because the system logs marked the task complete
questions.explanation: Salesforce classifies an agent that is technically accurate but not useful enough to let the user complete the task as a P1 intent failure. The scenario also illustrates a phantom success, where logs flag a win while the user experiences a loss, and the lesson warns these quiet failures push users back to old workflows.

questions.question: A board member asks how you keep an agent from calling the wrong tool or endpoint. Which response reflects the design discipline the lesson teaches for the tool-use layer?
options: Rely on the model's strong reasoning so it will pick the correct tool on its own
Trust the evaluation at the outcome layer, since final results confirm correctness
Present the tool schemas and semantic descriptions you wrote, and the evaluation that exercises tool selection against realistic inputs
Disable tool calls in production to eliminate the failure mode entirely
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that poorly defined tool schemas and vague semantic descriptions drive agents to invoke irrelevant APIs. The architect defends the tool contracts by showing the written schema and description for each tool and how tool selection was tested under realistic inputs.
